claims.text: Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles contain local compositional inhomogeneities.
Local compositional inhomogeneities create microregions with distinct melting points.
Lower-melting microregions cause partial melting to begin below the bulk melting temperature.
Melting proceeds as a two-stage transition in which lower-melting zones liquefy first and subsequently coalesce into a fully molten state.
The as-synthesized Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are nominally single-phase.
The Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles have sub-10-nm diameters.
Increasing the number of constituent elements promotes chemically mixed or random nanoparticles while still permitting local segregation.
Local chemical and bonding variations lower the energetic barrier to liquid nucleation in favored-composition regions.
As temperature increases, initially molten regions expand and coalesce into a uniform liquid.
Localized liquid pockets in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will appear at lower temperatures than in simpler reference particles of similar size.
The growth of localized liquid pockets will correlate with the most compositionally disparate domains.
More compositionally uniform or single-element nanoparticles will exhibit significantly delayed and less extensive partial melting.
Single-metal or basic bimetallic nanoparticles of similar size melt near their standard bulk melting points.
Single-metal or basic bimetallic nanoparticles display less pronounced premelting than Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Near-binary or strongly non-equiatomic compositions may show negligible or no early localized melting.
Larger particles have reduced surface-driven compositional inhomogeneity and may therefore show negligible or no early localized melting.
Heating rate and synthesis history may influence the observed melting profile.
Failure of partial melting to correlate with local composition, or observation of a melting profile identical to simpler references without early localized pockets, would falsify the hypothesis.
